stem: A professional handball club books four sessions meant to get players talking openly with one another about losing a starting place. The head coach says he'll help in whatever way is most useful. In individual meetings with the consultant, players had plenty to say. The coach then sat in on the first session: the room went quiet, the captain answered for everyone, and several players watched the coach before speaking. Which role should the consultant propose to the coach for the remaining sessions?
options: Leading the sessions himself, after briefings from the consultant
Joining the sessions as one voice among the players
Staying away from the sessions, which the consultant runs
Sitting in on the sessions, and cueing their skills in practice
rationales: Coach-led delivery can work when players look to the coach for guidance on the topic. These players fell silent merely because the coach, who decides who starts, was in the room.
Taking part as one voice assumes players will speak freely around the coach. In the first session they watched the coach before speaking and let the captain answer.

The sessions depend on open talk about selection, and the contrast between the individual meetings and the first session shows that the coach's presence shuts it down. A defined role outside the room best serves the program's aim.
Cueing skills in practice helps transfer when the program teaches a skill such as a reset. This program is about open conversation, and sitting in has already stifled it.
takeaway: Fit the coach's role to the aim of the sessions: presence that aids skill transfer can shut down open talk.

stem: At an intake meeting, Haruto, an elite golfer, describes a year with a former consultant: "I never missed a week. Within a month I had the breathing and the imagery down cold, and I did them in my room every night. Then I'd stand on the first tee of a tournament and have nothing. He told me to keep going, so I did the same thing for eleven more months." Which expectation about the new work is most important to set with Haruto?
options: His practice will move into harder and harder conditions
His gains will depend on work he does between sessions
His skills will need weeks of repetition to become steady
His nerves will remain, and he will learn to play with them
rationales: Haruto mastered the skills quickly in a quiet room and never practiced them anywhere else, so they didn't transfer. Skills need to be rehearsed under conditions that come to resemble competition, and he should expect that from the start.
Work between sessions is essential, but Haruto already did it every night for a year. Effort outside sessions wasn't what was missing.
This is the message for someone who quits after a few days. Haruto had the skills within a month and then repeated them for eleven more.
This expectation suits a client who judges a skill by whether nerves vanish. Haruto's complaint is that the skills themselves were unavailable on the tee.
takeaway: Mental skills learned in calm conditions must be practiced under pressure before they can be counted on there.

topic: Fitting a one-off workshop to its aim
stem: A logistics company's vice president asks a consultant for a single 90-minute workshop on mental performance for 200 employees. Asked what she'd like to be different afterward, she says, "We already fund individual sessions with your colleague, and the people who go rave about them. But most staff have never heard of it, or think it's therapy. I'd like them to walk out knowing what it is and how to book." How should the consultant respond to her request?
options: Propose a six-session series in place of the single workshop
Propose training for supervisors in place of the staff workshop
Suggest a needs survey of employees ahead of the workshop
Accept the workshop in the single-session form requested
rationales: A series is right when the aim is new skills that staff will use at work. The aim here is awareness of an existing service, which one session can deliver.
Training supervisors fits when the change depends on how supervisors act. The vice president wants staff themselves to know about a service and how to book it.
A survey is useful when nobody can say what employees need. She has named a clear gap in knowledge and a clear result she wants.
Her goal is informational: staff should know what a service is and how to book it. A single session is well matched to that goal, so the request needs no redesign.
takeaway: Match the format to the goal: a single workshop can build awareness, though it rarely builds skills.

stem: A high school athletic director is planning mental performance training with a consultant and describes last year's yoga program: "We made it mandatory, and attendance was perfect. The volleyball team had been asking for it, and they still do it on the bus. Football and wrestling lay on the mats and counted ceiling tiles until it ended. So I've already printed your sign-in sheets, every team, every Tuesday." Which point about mental performance training does the director most need to hear?
options: It serves performers of any level, including those doing well
It takes hold best with athletes who choose to take part
It builds skills gradually, through practice across a season
It teaches performance skills and is separate from clinical care
rationales: This point helps a director who reserves training for athletes in trouble. This director is already enrolling every team.

The same program lasted with the team that had asked for it and left no trace with those who were made to come. Willing participation drives learning and use of mental skills, so perfect attendance is the wrong target.
Gradual skill building is the message for someone who wants a quick fix. The director has planned weekly sessions, and the yoga failed with some teams and lasted with others.
This would matter if the director were confusing the training with counseling. The account of the yoga program raises no such confusion.
takeaway: Mandated attendance fills seats; voluntary commitment builds skills.

stem: A professional volleyball club hires a consultant for six hours a month, and the head coach expects a mental performance plan for each of 18 players. The consultant meets them all. Fourteen describe routines built over years, which match records show holding up in tight sets, and ask for nothing. The others each raise something: a server who rushes, a libero who dwells on bad passes, a setter new to starting, and a blocker who goes quiet in big arenas. How should the consultant propose to use the hours?
options: On team sessions for the full roster
On team sessions plus brief individual check-ins
On individual work for the players who ask
On a wider contract that gives each player a plan
rationales: Team sessions suit a need that players share. The four concerns differ from one another, and the rest of the roster is doing well.
A mixed model fits when there is a shared need alongside individual ones. The meetings turned up no shared need, so team time would draw hours from those who can use them.

The needs are individual, varied, and held by four willing players, while the others have routines that work. Matching delivery to assessed need makes good use of limited hours and resets the coach's expectation.
More hours would be worth requesting if most players wanted help. Fourteen don't, and their routines are holding up.
takeaway: Let assessed need, rather than roster size, decide how limited hours are spent.

topic: Agreeing on an aim for audition nerves
stem: Isabela, a professional violist, tells a consultant at intake that she wants her shaking dealt with before auditions. She has kept a diary of nine auditions. In four, her hands were fairly steady and she played well. In five, they shook hard and her bow skipped on the string. Her frame of mind didn't separate the two groups: before two of the five she had written, "Buzzing, can't wait, this one's mine." Which aim should the consultant propose for their work?
options: Reading the shaking as a sign that she is ready
Letting the shaking be there as she commits to the music
Making auditions more familiar through mock panels
Lowering the intensity of the shaking
rationales: Reinterpreting symptoms helps when the reading of them does the harm. Before two of the poor auditions she already read her state as excitement, and the bow skipped anyway.
Making room for symptoms suits a performer who plays well with them present. Her diary shows that hard shaking itself moves the bow, whatever her attitude.
Mock panels build familiarity when the setting is what unsettles a performer. Nothing in the diary ties the shaking to unfamiliar auditions.
Performance followed how hard her hands shook and not how she felt about it. For a fine motor task in which the symptom directly disrupts execution, lowering its intensity is the sensible aim.
takeaway: Interpretation matters, but when a symptom physically disrupts execution, reducing it is a sound aim.

stem: A collegiate men's basketball team learned a breathing-and-cue reset from its consultant in the fall. At the four road games the consultant attended, players came over before tip-off and again at halftime to be walked through it. At the five the consultant missed, video shows the same players using it without help at the same points. The coach offers a seat on the conference tournament trip and leaves the role open. Which role should the consultant propose?
options: Remaining at home, reachable by phone if needed
Staying near the team, available if players want to talk
Leading players through the reset ahead of each game
Helping coaches on the bench cue the reset in timeouts
rationales: Players run the reset themselves when the consultant is away and lean on the consultant when one is present. Staying home protects the independence the training was meant to build, and a call is still possible.
Being quietly available suits players who use their skills either way. These players come to the consultant whenever one is there, so being nearby invites the dependence.
Leading the reset would help players who forget it or can't manage it alone. Video from five games shows that they can.
Coach cues help when players miss the moments to use a skill. These players use it at the right points without prompting.
takeaway: Consulting aims at self-regulation; sometimes the most useful place to be is somewhere else.

stem: A mother signs the permission form and books ten sessions for Anselm, a 14-year-old figure skater, whose coach thinks he could be steadier in competition. At a first meeting the consultant described the work, and Anselm asked what a session would be like, who would hear about it, and whether he could have a week to think. Today he says, "I thought about it, and I get what it is. I don't want to do it." What should the consultant do next?
options: Explain to Anselm what the sessions would involve
End the intake without starting the sessions
Ask Anselm what he'd like to improve in his skating
Ask his mother what she has noticed in his skating
rationales: An explanation comes before a decision. Anselm asked good questions last time, got answers, and says he understands.
A minor's assent is sought alongside a guardian's permission. Anselm gave an informed, considered no to performance training, so the consultant respects it and can say that he is welcome back.
Exploring his goals suits a reluctant teenager who hasn't made up his mind. Anselm took a week and decided.
A parent's observations inform an assessment. There is no assessment to conduct until Anselm agrees to take part.
takeaway: For minors, guardian permission doesn't replace assent; a considered no should be honored.

stem: Moira, a 52-year-old triathlete, opens a video session by saying, "I need help with my race nutrition, and I know that isn't your department." She goes on: "In training I take a gel every half hour, the amounts my dietitian set, and they sit fine. In races, somebody passes me, I start chasing, and I find the gels in my pocket at the finish. My coach says I hold my pace well up to that point." How should the consultant handle the request?
options: Suggest she take it to her dietitian
Suggest she take it to a sports physician
Suggest she take it to her triathlon coach
Take it on in the sessions they have
rationales: A dietitian sets what and how much she eats, and that plan works in training. The trouble is that she forgets to follow it once she is chasing.
A physician would be the contact for symptoms such as dizziness or stomach pain. She reports none, and the gels sit fine.
A coach would handle pacing and training plans. Her pacing is sound until her attention goes to a rival.
The label is nutrition, but the pattern is a lapse in attention under competitive pressure. Helping her hold to an existing plan, with a cue or routine, is mental performance work.
takeaway: Judge scope by what is going wrong and not by the label a client gives it.

stem: A fire chief meets a consultant about mental performance training for the department. "I've paid for three of these," the chief says. "Crews signed up, they liked them, and nobody told me anyone's private business, which suits me fine. Each trainer said it had gone great. And I couldn't tell you one thing that was different at a fire the next month. I suppose you'll want six sessions as well?" What should the consultant settle with the chief first?
options: What the chief will hear about individual firefighters
How crews will learn that taking part is voluntary
What the chief would see if the training had worked
Where training ends and counseling would take over
rationales: Reporting limits come first when a chief expects to learn about individuals. This chief is content not to.
Voluntary participation would need settling if crews were being ordered to come. They signed up for the earlier programs willingly.

Three programs ended with nobody able to say what had changed, and the chief is about to buy a fourth the same way. Agreeing at the outset on observable outcomes gives the program an aim and something to judge it by.
The line with counseling matters when the request mixes the two, as after a traumatic call. The chief's complaint is about visible results.
takeaway: Agree on what success would look like before agreeing on the number of sessions.

stem: Bastian, a collegiate tennis player, has spent fifteen minutes on imagery every night since August. The pictures are clear, he can feel the racquet in his hand, and the ball goes where he sends it. His coach wonders why none of it has helped him believe he can win close matches. Asked what he works on, Bastian says, "Tennis stuff. Whatever comes up." Which instrument would tell the consultant most about the coach's question?
options: Movement Imagery Questionnaire-3 (MIQ-3)
Sport Imagery Questionnaire (SIQ)
Test of Performance Strategies (TOPS)
Athletic Coping Skills Inventory-28 (ACSI-28)
rationales: The MIQ-3 measures how well a person forms visual and kinesthetic images. Bastian's are already clear, felt, and under his control.

The SIQ shows which functions an athlete's imagery serves, such as rehearsing skills or building mastery and confidence. Bastian images well and often, so what his imagery is for is the open question.
The TOPS shows how often strategies, including imagery, are used in practice and competition. How often he uses imagery is already known.
The ACSI-28 profiles coping skills such as concentration and peaking under pressure. It wouldn't show what he does in his imagery.
takeaway: The MIQ-3 measures imagery ability; the SIQ shows what imagery is used for.

stem: With a parent's permission and her assent, a consultant has spent three weeks assessing Petra, a 16-year-old hockey goaltender. In the four games watched, Petra dropped deep into her net for several minutes after each soft goal. "I back up because I'm scared of the next one," she says. Her goalie coach, asked separately, describes the same thing and explains why it leaves shooters more net. Petra says it's what she wants to change. What should the consultant do next?
options: Give her a coping skills inventory to round out the picture
Watch more games to see whether the pattern holds
Learn more from the goalie coach about the position
Move on to setting goals and planning
rationales: An inventory can open up areas that a client can't describe. Petra has put the problem in plain words, and two other sources match.
More observation is worthwhile when a pattern rests on one or two sightings. This one appeared after soft goals across four games.
Learning the position's demands matters early on. The coach has already explained what the retreat costs her.
Interview, observation, and coach report converge on one specific pattern that Petra wants to change. Assessment has done its job, and the next stage is goals and planning.
takeaway: When independent sources converge and the client agrees, stop assessing and start planning.

stem: The coach of Ama, a collegiate pole vaulter, sums her up in one breath: she maps out each meet in a notebook, goes stony when he corrects her, loses the whole afternoon if she misses her opening height, and vaults her best in finals. Ama agrees to fill in one short questionnaire before her first interview. The consultant wants its subscales to speak to as much of that picture as possible. Which instrument fits best?
options: Athletic Coping Skills Inventory-28 (ACSI-28)
Competitive State Anxiety Inventory-2 (CSAI-2)
Test of Performance Strategies (TOPS)
Sport Imagery Questionnaire (SIQ)
rationales: The ACSI-28 includes goal setting and mental preparation, coachability, coping with adversity, and peaking under pressure. Those subscales line up with the notebook, the response to correction, the missed height, and the finals.
The CSAI-2 measures anxiety and self-confidence at a given moment, usually shortly before competing. It has nothing on taking correction or planning.
The TOPS measures use of strategies such as self-talk, relaxation, and goal setting in practice and competition. It would miss how she takes coaching.
The SIQ measures what an athlete uses imagery for. Imagery isn't part of the coach's description.
takeaway: The ACSI-28 profiles coping skills, including coachability, adversity, and peaking under pressure.

stem: At a video intake, professional esports player Junho, sent by his coach, announces, "I'm not really a mental training guy," and says scrims fill his day. As they talk, he mentions that he put a breathing app on his phone last week and has tried it twice, that a teammate is showing him a clutch-round routine tomorrow, and that he's blocked off ten minutes before Monday's scrim for one of his own. In the transtheoretical model, which reading of his readiness fits best?
options: Precontemplation, which calls for raising his awareness
Contemplation, which calls for weighing pros and cons
Preparation, which calls for settling a workable plan
Action, which calls for support and a guard against lapses
rationales: His opening line sounds like precontemplation, but people in that stage have no intention to change soon. He has a start set for Monday.
Contemplation means thinking about change while still undecided. He has moved past deciding and is arranging how to begin.
He intends to begin within days and has taken small steps toward it, which marks preparation. Help at this stage goes into a concrete plan that he can start.
In action, a person is already carrying out the new behavior. Two tries with an app fall short of that, and his routine has yet to start.
takeaway: Read readiness from intentions and steps taken as well as from how clients describe themselves.

stem: In scenario training, a SWAT officer's hands tremble at door keypads, and his radio calls speed up until dispatch asks him to repeat them. He rates himself "calm" each time. When an instructor showed him his heart-rate trace, he pointed out that he'd just run three flights in full kit, which was true. The scenarios are recorded on body cameras. Which method would best help him notice what his instructors notice?
options: Interview him about the scenarios he finds hardest
Review his footage and radio audio with him
Track his heart rate and compare it with his ratings
Give him a trait anxiety inventory and discuss the scores
rationales: An interview draws on what he is already aware of. He believes he is calm, so his account will repeat that.

Trembling hands and rushed speech can be seen and heard on the recordings, and exertion doesn't explain them away so easily. Reviewing them with him lets him compare his ratings with his own behavior.
Heart rate rises with effort as well as stress, and he has already explained the trace by the stairs. More of the same data invites the same reply.
A trait inventory shows how anxious he generally says he is. It relies on the self-report that is in question and says little about behavior in scenarios.
takeaway: Choose an assessment whose data speak directly to the gap between self-view and behavior.

stem: Solveig, a collegiate water polo player, scores high on the concentration subscale of the ACSI-28. Her coach says she loses her defensive assignment late in close games and puts it down to nerves. Charting eight games, the consultant finds nearly all her lapses in the fourth quarter, as many with a six-goal lead as with the score tied. In the two games when early fouls kept her on the bench through the third quarter, she had none. Which explanation fits the evidence best?
options: She tires in the later stages of games
She feels the pressure when games are close
She is unsure of parts of the defensive scheme
She rates her concentration too favorably
rationales: The lapses follow time in the water: they come late, whatever the score, and vanish when she has rested. Fatigue accounts for the pattern and for how a player with good concentration skills could still lose her assignment.
This is the coach's view, but a tied score brought no more lapses than a six-goal lead.
Confusion about the scheme would show up throughout games. She had hardly any lapses before the fourth quarter and none when rested.
A generous self-rating might explain a mismatch between score and behavior, but it wouldn't explain why the lapses come late and disappear after a rest.
takeaway: Look for the condition that comes and goes with the problem before choosing a target.

stem: A consultant who has trained, traveled, and eaten with a collegiate women's rowing crew all month would have called them close, and so would their coach. But on anonymous Group Environment Questionnaires, half of the 18 rowers rate the crew's unity around its task near the bottom of the scale and half rate it near the top. The coach has a team-building retreat booked in three weeks and asks what should happen before it. Which step should the consultant take next?
options: Plan the retreat around shared goals for the season
Repeat the questionnaire after the crew's next race
Observe practices and meals over the next two weeks
Talk privately with rowers about how they see the crew
rationales: Shared goals may turn out to be the right focus, but nobody yet knows what splits the crew. Planning now would be a guess.
Repeating the measure would show whether scores change over time. It can't show why half the crew rates it low.
Observation suits a consultant who has yet to see the crew together. This one has watched them for a month and missed the split.

The questionnaire shows a deep split that isn't visible from outside, and anonymous forms can't say what lies behind it. Private conversations can bring out reasons that rowers don't show in the group.
takeaway: Questionnaires show where a problem lies; conversations help show why.

stem: Six weeks into an imagery plan for composure, Anjali, a collegiate pianist, asks her consultant for something different because her jury was "a mess." Her log shows four imagery sessions a week, as agreed. The jury fell in the second week. In weekly studio class, where she plays for about thirty students and faculty, her composure ratings have run 3, 3, 4, 5, 5, 6. Her next jury is a month away. What should the consultant recommend?
options: Keep the imagery plan as it is until the next jury
Replace the imagery with a cue-word strategy
Work out what has kept her from imagery sessions
Move her imagery into rehearsals with an audience
rationales: The one poor result came before the plan had had time to work, and ratings in front of an audience have climbed steadily since. With practice on track and a fair test a month off, the evidence supports staying the course.
Changing strategies makes sense when a well-practiced plan shows no benefit. Her studio class ratings have doubled.
Barriers need exploring when practice is being missed. Her log shows every agreed session.
Adding pressure helps when gains stop short of performance settings. Hers already appear when she plays for an audience.
takeaway: Judge a plan on adherence and the trend, not on one result from its first days.

stem: Corwin, a collegiate swimmer, set a goal of holding a target stroke rate on 8 of 10 repeats in Thursday's set. Over five weeks he has managed 8, 10, 10, 10, and 10. "Best part of my week," he says. "I'd like to keep it just like this, it's great for my confidence." His coach mentions that Corwin has started chatting between repeats and that his attention drifts in the second half of the set. What is the most appropriate adjustment?
options: Leave the stroke-rate goal at its current level
Ease the stroke-rate goal to a smaller step
Make the stroke-rate goal harder to reach
Pair the stroke-rate goal with a race-time goal
rationales: Keeping the goal would suit a swimmer still working to reach it. Four perfect weeks and wandering attention show that it no longer asks much of him.
A smaller step helps a swimmer who keeps falling short. Corwin has met his goal every week.
Challenging goals draw more effort and attention than easy ones. He reaches this one with little effort and his attention drifts, so raising the standard restores its value.
Linking it to race times helps a swimmer who can't see the point of the goal. Corwin values it; it has simply become easy.
takeaway: A goal that is met without effort has stopped directing effort; raise it.

stem: After a six-week stress-management program, paramedics rate the sessions highly, and nearly all perform the breathing and refocusing techniques well in the drills that open each shift. On ride-alongs, supervisors see the techniques on about one call in ten. "I believe in it," one medic says, "I've felt it work. I just think of it when I'm restocking the rig." Which revision to the program fits these findings best?
options: Reteach the techniques with closer demonstration and feedback
Pair one technique with a step crews take on each call
Add time for technique practice to the start of shifts
Have respected medics describe how the techniques helped
rationales: Reteaching addresses weak skills. Crews perform the techniques well in drills.
Crews can use the techniques and want to, but they remember too late. Tying one to a step already in every call, such as pulling on gloves, puts a reminder at the moment of use.
More practice time helps when skills have gone rusty. Crews already practice at the start of each shift and perform well.
Testimony from peers helps when crews doubt the techniques. The medic already believes in them and has felt them work.
takeaway: When skill and belief are present but use is not, build a cue into the job itself.

stem: For six weeks Emre, an elite judo athlete, has used slow diaphragmatic breathing at competitions. He now sleeps well before tournaments, and his activation ratings as he bows in are where he likes them. Yet he has lost three matches early on grips. On video he is a beat late to each opponent's first reach. "I keep the breath low and slow the whole way through," he says, "just like we practiced." How should the consultant adjust the plan?
options: Add a cognitive strategy for the night before tournaments
Lengthen the breathing he does before each match
Confine the breathing to the time before he bows in
Replace the breathing with an activating routine
rationales: A cognitive strategy would address pre-tournament worry. He sleeps well before tournaments.
Longer breathing would suit an athlete who is still too keyed up at the start. His ratings are where he wants them.

The breathing does its job before matches, but he carries it into the fight, where it holds his attention on his own body as the opponent moves. Keeping it to the preparation period preserves the benefit and frees his attention.
Activation would help if the breathing had left him flat. He reaches the mat at his preferred level, and the trouble begins once the match does.
takeaway: A well-learned technique can hurt when it takes attention at the wrong moment.

stem: In the first month of base training, Kavya, a collegiate distance runner, shows her consultant a log full of process goals for stride, pacing, and recovery. She checks them off daily, and her training times are improving. Still, she has begun cutting warm-ups short. "I know exactly what I'm doing tomorrow," she says. "I couldn't tell you what I'm doing it for." She perks up once, when a teammate's hopes for nationals come up. Which addition to her goals fits best?
options: Process goals for her focus during races
Performance goals for her times at each meet
An outcome goal for her place at nationals
A weekly review of the goals she already has
rationales: Process goals help when a runner is caught up in rivals or results. Kavya's log is full of them, and the daily work isn't what she lacks.
Times give a runner standards for judging progress. Her times are already improving, and what she lacks is a reason that stirs her.
Outcome goals can supply long-range direction and drive, particularly far from competition. Her day-to-day goals are in place, and the prospect of nationals is what lifts her.
A review would help if she were forgetting or ignoring her goals. She checks them off every day.
takeaway: Process goals steer the work; a distant outcome goal can give it a purpose.

stem: Marlon, an elite sprinter, has run below his best since joining a new club, whose sprinters warm up together with loud music, shouting, and chest slaps. His coach, sure that sprinters need firing up, wants more of it. Marlon has rated his bodily activation from 1 to 10 before every race for two years. His five fastest races carry ratings of 3 or 4; this season's ratings run from 7 to 9. His mind, he says, is "quiet as ever." Which routine should his plan prioritize?
options: An energizing routine of music, quick breaths, and power words
A restructuring routine for his thoughts about the race
A refocusing routine built on cues from the lane and blocks
A settling routine of slow breathing and muscle release
rationales: Energizing is the familiar choice for sprinters and would suit one who was flat. Marlon is already far above the level of his best races.
Restructuring targets worry. He describes a quiet mind.
Refocusing helps when attention wanders. He reports nothing of the kind, while his activation has changed sharply.

Individual zones can sit at any intensity, whatever the event's reputation. His best races came at low activation and his current ratings are roughly double, so a somatic settling routine moves him back toward his zone.
takeaway: An athlete's own records, rather than the sport's reputation, set the target for arousal.

stem: A collegiate softball coach gives a consultant 15 minutes of team time a week. "My two pitchers fall apart after errors," the coach says. The consultant charts six games. After an error, the pitchers' speed and location stay the same. Balls put in play by the next few batters are misplayed more than usual, by infielders and outfielders alike, and the usual chatter between fielders stops. Where should the plan place its work?
options: With the whole team, on regrouping after an error
With the two pitchers, on a reset between batters
With the pitching coach, on what to say at mound visits
With the infielders, on recovering from a misplay
rationales: The charts show that pitching holds up while fielding and talk suffer across the field. The need is shared by the team, so team time spent on a collective response fits best.
The coach named the pitchers, but their speed and location don't change after errors.
Mound visits reach the pitchers, who are holding steady, and leave out the fielders, who aren't.
The infielders are affected, but the outfielders are too, and the loss of talk runs through the whole defense.
takeaway: Let the data, not the referral, show at which level the problem lies.

stem: Philippa, a recreational archer, shoots 144 arrows on competition day. Video of a recent event shows the same clean release from first arrow to last, whenever she completes the shot. In the final thirty arrows, though, she keeps easing off halfway through the draw and starting again, and she runs short of time. "My back is burning and I think, I can't hold this bow anymore," she says. Which cue should her self-talk plan use for those arrows?
options: A technique cue, such as "smooth release"
An effort cue, such as "strong, keep pulling"
A calming cue, such as "soft and easy"
An attention cue, such as "eyes on gold"
rationales: Instructional cues suit precision and technique, and archery brings them to mind. Her release stays clean, though, so there is no fault for the cue to correct.
What fails late in the day is strength endurance and the will to finish the draw. Motivational self-talk suits strength and endurance demands and answers the thought that she can't hold on.
A calming cue would help if she were tense or rushed. She is tired, and a softer pull is the problem.
An attention cue would help if her focus left the target. It is the draw that stops, as her muscles burn.
takeaway: Match self-talk to the demand that is failing at that moment, not to the sport's label.

stem: Leandro, an elite wheelchair racer training abroad for three months, meets his consultant by video every two weeks. For six weeks he has followed a recorded pre-race routine of breathing and imagery each day, and on camera he does it well. Last week, his phone died just before a time trial. "I got through the first breath," he says, "and then I had no idea what came next." What should the plan emphasize for practice between sessions?
options: Recorded guidance that he follows on his own
Run-throughs from memory, with no recording
Extra rehearsals with the consultant by video
Cueing from his coach at the training base
rationales: Recordings are a good support for learning between distant sessions. He has had six weeks of them and can't run the routine when they are gone.
He performs well with the recording and can't recall the sequence without it, so the support has become a crutch. Practicing unaided builds a routine he can carry to the start line.
Extra live rehearsals would correct his technique, which is already good. They would also keep the prompts coming from outside.
A coach's cues would replace one external prompt with another. He needs to be able to run it without either.
takeaway: Use recordings to teach a routine, and then fade them so that the athlete owns it.

stem: The coach of a collegiate esports team sets a goal for the semester: "communicate better." In recordings of lost matches, the consultant hears calls that are prompt, frequent, and clear. Again and again, though, a player calls a move, pauses, and makes it alone, or two players turn up at the same spot. Afterward there are exchanges such as "I told you!" and "I know, I was coming!" Which specific goal fits best?
options: Make at least 20 calls in each round
Make 90 percent of sighting calls within two seconds
Cut calls unrelated to the current play by half
Answer 90 percent of teammates' calls out loud
rationales: A count of calls helps a quiet team. These players already call often.
A speed standard helps when information arrives late. The calls on the recordings are prompt.
Trimming helps when useful calls are buried in chatter. The calls on the recordings are clear.
Calls are made and heard, but the caller can't tell, so players act on guesses. A measurable goal for answering calls targets the missing part of the exchange.
takeaway: A specific goal helps when it targets the behavior that assessment shows to be missing.

stem: Suyin, an elite springboard diver, shows her consultant the nine goals she has written for a training block. The first reads, "Spot the water early on 8 of 10 reverse dives by March 1," and the others follow the same form. She likes them and records her numbers after each practice, yet her coach says her dives have become hesitant. "I stand on the board going through them," Suyin says, "and then I'm in the air." Which revision fits best?
options: Work on one of the goals in each practice
Reword the goals as what she wants to do
Attach a measure of success to each goal
Set a date for reaching each of the goals
rationales: Her goals are well formed, but she tries to hold nine in mind on the board. Narrowing to one at a time gives her attention a single task at takeoff.
Rewording helps when goals name what to avoid. Hers already say what she will do.
A measure helps when progress can't be judged. Hers carry numbers, and she records them.
Dates help when goals drift. Hers already have them.
takeaway: Well-written goals can still fail when there are too many to attend to at once.

stem: A high school volleyball coach wants players to have a dependable pre-serve routine after six weekly sessions. Last season the same players learned a breath, a cue word, and a brief image of the serve in separate units. When the consultant asks for each in the first meeting, nearly all the players do it well. In scrimmages, however, no player prepares the same way twice, and serving drops off when the score is tight. Which sequence fits best?
options: Reteach each skill on its own, then combine them later
Track serving under pressure, then let players choose skills
Combine the skills in week one, then rehearse in tougher drills
Set serving goals for the team, then teach skills to match
rationales: Building from the parts is sound for beginners. These players already do each part well, so it would spend most of the six weeks on what they know.
Tracking first helps when the problem is unclear. The scrimmages have already shown what happens and when.
The parts are learned, and what is missing is a consistent whole that holds up under pressure. Assembling it at once leaves five weeks to rehearse it in drills that grow more demanding.
Goals first would help players who lacked direction. The coach's aim is clear, and the players already have the skills that serve it.
takeaway: Start a program from what learners can already do.

stem: Chiamaka, an elite fencer, keeps attacking in close bouts, though her stomach churns. "That's just fencing," she shrugs. What costs her touches is a line that arrives at 13–13: You always choke. "And then I'm in court," she tells her consultant, who works from acceptance and commitment therapy. "I'm building my whole case against it, and the other fencer scores." Which ACT process should the plan stress?
options: Defusion, to see the line as words her mind produces
Values work, to name the fencer she wants to be
Acceptance, to make room for what she feels in her body
Committed action, to take set steps toward attacking
rationales: She is caught up in the content of a thought, arguing with it as if it had to be settled before she could fence. Defusion changes how she relates to the thought, so that it can come without a trial.
Values work helps when an athlete has lost sight of what matters in how she competes. Her trouble is a thought that captures her attention.
Acceptance helps when an athlete struggles against feelings or sensations. She already lets her churning stomach be and fences on.
Committed action helps when avoidance keeps an athlete from what she values. She keeps attacking.
takeaway: When a client is busy arguing with a thought, defusion is the ACT process to reach for.

stem: Players on an elite women's field hockey team prepare for matches on their own, as each sees fit. The coach, concerned about slow starts, asks the consultant for a plan. For ten matches, players have rated their activation on a 10-point scale at the opening whistle. Sorting each player's ratings by how well she played, the consultant finds the best performances of all 18 players between 6 and 8. Typical ratings before this season's matches are 3 to 5. Which plan fits these data best?
options: Individual routines that each player designs
A calming routine for some and an energizing one for others
A short shared opening, then time for individual routines
A single energizing routine for the whole squad
rationales: Individual routines fit when players' best levels differ widely. These players' best levels cluster, and preparing alone has left most below them.
Two groups would fit if some players did best at low levels. All 18 did best between 6 and 8.
A shared opening with individual time suits a squad with varied needs. This squad shares one need, and time alone is how players came to start flat.
Individual zones have to be assessed, and here they turn out to be much the same. Nearly everyone is starting below that range, so one energizing routine serves the whole squad.
takeaway: Individual zones are a matter for assessment: sometimes a squad's zones coincide.

stem: Caleb, a collegiate pitcher, added a slider over the winter. The team physician has him off throwing for two weeks, until just before the opener. "I know the pitch is good," he tells his consultant. "It just isn't a pitch for someone five-nine with a low arm slot, not in this conference." His coach keeps telling him how nasty it looks, and Caleb nods politely. According to self-efficacy theory, what should his confidence plan feature during the layoff?
options: Graded tasks that let him succeed with the slider step by step
Encouragement about the slider from someone whose eye he trusts
Film of pitchers built like him who succeed with the slider
Practice in reading his pregame jitters as readiness
rationales: Mastery experiences are the strongest source, but he can't throw for two weeks. They belong in the plan once he is cleared.
Persuasion is the weakest fit here: he already agrees that the pitch is good and shrugs off praise. His doubt is about pitchers like himself.

He doubts that someone with his build and delivery can succeed. Seeing similar others succeed is vicarious experience, whose influence grows with the model's similarity, and it is available while he can't throw.
Reinterpreting bodily signs helps when arousal is taken as a sign of failure to come. He hasn't mentioned any such signs.
takeaway: Mastery is the strongest source of efficacy, but a similar model is the fit when doubt centers on 'people like me.'

stem: Last year a software company put two-minute mindfulness exercises into its product launch meetings. Managers enjoyed them and kept turning up, but by autumn the habit had faded. "It's like doing one push-up," says one. "Nice, and then the day eats it." Twenty managers have now asked their consultant, a trained mindfulness teacher, for help staying steady under launch pressure, and the company has cleared two hours a week for them through the spring. Which plan fits this group best?
options: Brief attention exercises tied to tasks in launch meetings
The standard eight-week MBSR course, taught as designed
A research briefing, followed by optional taster sessions
A self-guided app, with a group check-in each month
rationales: Brief, task-linked exercises suit busy managers who are wary of meditation. This group had a year of them and found them too slight to last.
The managers want more than small doses, have asked for help themselves, and have the hours. A full course with sustained practice fits both their request and their resources.
A briefing suits managers who doubt the evidence. These managers have tried the practice, liked it, and come back for more.
An app suits people who can't meet or who want to work alone. This group has protected time together and a trained teacher.
takeaway: Adapt the dose to the group: shorter isn't better for people who want, and have time for, depth.

stem: A performance profile done with Sienna, a collegiate dance major, shows gaps between her current and target ratings in six areas. Her company audition is ten months away, time enough to get to all six. She has dropped two earlier programs within a month of starting. "I go straight for the big scary thing," she says. "Nothing moves, I decide I'm hopeless, and I stop." Which area should the plan take up first?
options: The area with the widest gap between ratings
The area she rates as most important
The area her director sees as most pressing
The area closest to its target rating
rationales: Starting with the widest gap is a common reading of a profile. It is also what she has done twice, and slow movement led her to quit.
Importance is often the best guide when time is short. With ten months in hand, the greater risk is another early exit.
A director's view can help set priorities. It doesn't touch what has ended her earlier programs.
Her history shows that a lack of early progress ends her programs. The smallest gap is likeliest to close soon, and an early success builds the efficacy to continue to the harder areas.
takeaway: When early discouragement is the main threat, begin where success will come soonest.

stem: Omar, a professional squash player, is about to restart a between-rally refocusing routine. The first time, his consultant charted the points he won right after losing one. Over two months the figure didn't move, and they dropped the routine. Omar has since gone back through the match video. "Most of the time I just wiped my hand on the wall and walked back to the box," he says. Which measure should the new plan track first?
options: How often he runs the routine between rallies
How focused he feels as each rally begins
How many points he wins right after losing one
How many matches he wins across the season
rationales: The first attempt judged the routine's effect without checking that it took place, and the video suggests it mostly didn't. Tracking use first shows whether there is anything to evaluate.
Focus ratings would show what he experiences. They can't be credited to a routine until he is known to be running it.
This is a sensible effect measure, and it was the one used before. It stayed flat because the routine was seldom run.
Match results reflect opponents, fitness, and much else. They are furthest from the question that the video raises.
takeaway: Check that a skill is being used before judging whether it works.

stem: A consultant follows a masters golfer for nine holes. Before each shot he checks the lie and the wind, names a club and a shot shape without fuss, steps up, fixes his eyes on a spot in the fairway, and swings. "I know what I want, and I'm looking right where it should go," he says, "but the swing that comes out is always a surprise to me." Using Nideffer's model, which step would be most useful to add to his routine?
options: A broad-external step, to take in the lie and the conditions
A broad-internal step, to settle on a club and a shot
A narrow-internal step, to rehearse how the swing will feel
A narrow-external step, to lock on to a target
rationales: Reading conditions comes first in many routines, and he already does it.
Planning the shot is the analytic step. He names a club and shape with ease.

He goes from plan to target with no rehearsal of the movement between them, and the swing surprises him. A narrow-internal step is suited to mentally rehearsing the swing before he shifts out to the target.
Locking on to a target is the execution step. He already fixes on a spot before swinging.
takeaway: A routine can move through each attentional style in turn; look for the one that is skipped.

stem: A youth soccer club wants mental skills training for its 9- to 11-year-olds, who "fall apart after mistakes" in matches. At two practices, the consultant sees the children lose the ball, laugh, and chase it. At Saturday's match, the consultant charts every turnover. In the first half, eleven children lose the ball in midfield, and nine of them are substituted within a minute. In the second half, most passes go backward. With whom should the plan begin?
options: The players, with short games that build a reset habit
The coaches, with guidance on responding to errors
The parents, with a meeting on sideline support
The older players, as mentors who model recovery
rationales: Short, active games suit this age, and they would be a good start if the children couldn't recover from mistakes. In practice they recover happily.
The children cope well until a lost ball means coming off, and then they stop risking passes. The coaches' response to errors is the condition that changed, so it is where the plan should begin.
A parent meeting would fit if the sideline were reacting to mistakes. What follows the turnovers is a substitution.
Models help children who haven't seen how to recover. These children already do so at practice.
takeaway: With children, look at how adults respond to mistakes before teaching the children to cope.
